Task: Write a quick note explaining why TCP differs from UDP.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) are both transport-layer protocols, but they differ fundamentally in how they deliver data:

• Reliability: TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery. It establishes a connection, numbers packets (segments), requires acknowledgments, retransmits lost segments, and uses flow-control mechanisms like sliding windows. UDP is connectionless and “best effort”: it simply wraps data in datagrams and sends them without guaranteeing delivery, order, or integrity beyond an optional checksum.

• Overhead vs. speed: Because TCP manages connections, acknowledgments, and congestion control, it introduces more overhead and latency. UDP’s minimal header (8 bytes vs. TCP’s 20+ bytes) and lack of connection setup make it faster and more suitable for real-time applications (e.g., VoIP, online gaming) where occasional loss is acceptable.

• Congestion and flow control: TCP dynamically adjusts its sending rate to avoid network congestion, whereas UDP leaves congestion handling to the application or the network, which can lead to packet loss if the path is overloaded.

• Use cases: TCP is preferred for applications where accuracy matters—web browsing, file transfers, email—while UDP is chosen for time-sensitive scenarios where speed outweighs reliability.
